newsitem.title: CHINA: Japanese landing on dispute isles sparks fury.
newsitem.headline: Japanese landing on dispute isles sparks fury.

text.p: China and Taiwan reacted with anger on Tuesday to a visit by a Japanese nationalist legislator to disputed islands in the East China Sea, while the Japanese government quickly distanced itself from the landing.
Hong Kong activists backing China's claims to the Japanese administered isles pledged to go ahead with plans to sail to the islands from Taiwan with Taiwanese protesters on May 18.
Tuesday's incident, which saw conservative Japanese deputy Shingo Nishimura and three other other people land on the Diaoyu, or Senkaku islands, threatened to rekindle a decades old dispute.
"The Chinese side expresses its strong indignation and opposition," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing in Beijing.
"The illegal landing...is a serious violation of China's territorial sovereignty," Shen said. "The Diaoyu islands have been a part of Chinese territory since ancient times."
In Taipei the Taiwan Foreign Ministry expressed "grave concern" over Nishimura's visit.
"We urge Japan to exercise self-restraint and not to create any trouble that will affect our friendly relations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Roy Wu told a news conference.
More than a dozen Hong Kong activists staged a noisy protest outside Japan's consulate in the island's financial district to condemn the landing on the islands as a revival of Japanese militarism.
Japan, which has claimed the islands between Taiwan and Okinawa since 1895, was quick to distance itself from the landing by Nishimura, a member of the main opposition New Frontier Party.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, clearly displeased, told reporters: "It is well-known that the owner of the land has refused to allow landings there. Do members of parliament have the right to completely ignore that?"

Other top officials appealed for calm over the dispute, which last year exploded into fiery anti-Japanese demonstrations in Hong Kong and Taiwan after a Japanese right-wing group built a small lighthouse on one of the islands.

"The government will calmly deal with the issue, as countries which are taking standpoints different from Japan are also dealing with it calmly," Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told a news conference.

Nishimura's group, which held a brief ceremony on the island, sailed on a chartered vessel carrying cameras, video recording equipment and a Japanese flag, his parliamentary office said in a statement.

"We believe this landing on the Senkaku Islands will be the starting point for an awakening of national consciousness and the rebirth of a Japan with pride," the statement said in a pointed challenge to the Tokyo government.
The issue of the islands, which lie 1,600 km (1,000 miles) southwest of Tokyo, languished as an obscure dispute until the construction of the lighthouse last July.

Taiwanese and Hong Kong Chinese protestors launched a series of flotilla protests over several months. Several activists landed briefly on the islands, which are administered from Japan's Okinawa province.
Last September, a Hong Kong activist drowned when he jumped into stormy waters near the islands to press China's claim.
